## Slide 2 · Part I: Organization & outlook

Presenter note: say a word about how to use these slides. They are deliberately
kept lean — every slide carries only the keywords, the elaboration happens in
the session itself, in the accompanying videos and in the written tutorials on
the course website. Students should not treat the slide deck alone as a
complete script.

## Slide 3 · The goal of the implementation lab

The goal of the implementation lab is that you learn how to prepare, analyse and
present quantitative data using R, and that you implement all the tools covered
in the main lecture practically.

These three activities are not a sequence you walk through once. Data
preparation, visualisation and modelling feed back into each other constantly:
a first plot shows you that the data are still messy, a model result sends you
back to the preparation step, and so on. Everything then funnels into the last
step — presenting the insights as one coherent story.

## Slide 4 · Why R?

R allows you to conduct all steps of this data science pipeline within one
consistent framework, in a transparent and reproducible manner.

R is free, OS-independent and open source, which makes it an inclusive,
transparent and vibrant tool.

For statistical analysis, R is among the most widely used and demanded
programming languages. The table on the right is worth a minute, because it
makes a methodological point as well as a substantive one: R is #4, #9 and #13
at the same time, depending on the index.

The three indices count different things. PYPL counts how often people search
for *tutorials*, so it captures who is currently **learning** a language — and
there R is #4 worldwide. TIOBE counts search-result volume, i.e. general
visibility, and puts R at #9. RedMonk combines GitHub code with Stack Overflow
discussion, i.e. general engineering activity, where web and systems languages
dominate the traffic — there R is #13. R is a specialised statistical language,
so it sits near the top of the learning-oriented index and further down the
engineering-oriented one. A metric's sampling frame determines its result; that
is a lesson worth carrying into the rest of the course.

The trend matters too: in TIOBE, R climbed from #15 in early 2025 to #9, which
TIOBE attributes to specialised languages reclaiming ground from Python.

R is demanded in almost every industry, learning R makes it easier to learn
other widely used programming languages afterwards, and there is a great and
friendly R community that you can turn to when you get stuck.

## Slide 5 · What you will be able to do — read & tidy data

Concretely, by the end of the semester you will be able to read in data sets
from various sources — from the European Commission, the OECD, the World Bank,
the IMF or the German Federal Statistical Office, among many others. Each of
them publishes data in its own format and its own logic.

You will then be able to prepare such 'messy' data and turn them into 'tidy'
data: the raw comma-separated file at the top becomes the structured table at
the bottom, where every column is a variable and every row an observation. That
tidy form is the precondition for everything that follows.

## Slide 6 · What you will be able to do — visualise & model

You will also be able to create illustrative visualisations on a
publication-ready level. The bubble chart here relates GDP per capita to life
expectancy; the size of each bubble is the population of the country and the
colour its continent. It is produced in a handful of lines of R code, and it is
fully reproducible — re-running the script with updated data gives you an
updated figure.

Beyond describing the data, you will use models to identify patterns that are
not visible to the naked eye and to make predictions.

## Slide 7 · What you will be able to do — report & publish

A third block concerns communication. You will write reproducible research
reports in Quarto: code, results and text live in one single file, so a figure
in your report can never get out of sync with the data it came from.

You will publish visually appealing reports on the web via Netlify — literally
by dragging the output folder into the browser.

And all of this is not specific to this course: you learn tools and methods that
will be required in subsequent seminars, and in your thesis.

## Slide 8 · But can't ChatGPT just do this for us…?

A question that comes up every year: can't ChatGPT just do all of this for us?
The answer is yes and no.

LLMs such as ChatGPT can be very useful when developing code. But the benefit
depends entirely on your own level. If you know a programming language well,
LLMs boost your productivity considerably. If you do not know the language well,
LLMs will mostly confuse you: they often return slightly misbehaving code, so
you always need to work on the output; they do not know the most recent
developments in the language; and their code is not always easy to read.

We will learn the basics of using LLMs for coding, and you can always use them,
including during the exam — but be wary of their limitations.

## Slide 9 · Organization of the lab sessions

Each on-site session comprises theory and practice, so always bring your
laptops. Some topics are presented better by instructional videos; for those
sessions, watch the videos, do the exercises, and pose your questions.

Questions should always be posted online in the Moodle forum. They should
primarily be answered by fellow students — helping one another with problems
greatly enhances your own understanding. The forum also ensures that answers to
questions are, first, recorded, and second, available to everybody. Particularly
intriguing questions can be discussed at the beginning of a session.

## Slide 11 · Our 'learning agreement'

Why do I expect regular activities from you?

Learning a programming language is a consecutive activity: if you miss the
basics in the beginning, you will quickly become frustrated and get lost. This
is a demanding course, and catching up later on what you missed earlier will be
difficult.

Learning a programming language works mainly through practice and doing, so the
practical exercises have a huge benefit. It is also difficult and at times
frustrating, which is why we need an amicable environment and must support each
other. And few things have a bigger learning effect than helping others with
their problems.

## Slide 14 · R and R-Studio — language vs. IDE

Two pieces of software, and they are often confused.

R is a programming language. It is a language that allows you to issue commands
to your computer: you write `fib_n(4)`, R translates that into something the
machine actually understands, and hands you back the result — here, the number 3.

R Studio is an integrated development environment, an IDE. It is basically a
fancy text editor with a lot of additional features that make programming easy:
a script editor, a console, an overview of the objects in your environment, and
a pane for plots and help files.

## Slide 15 · R and R-Studio — engine & dashboard

Ismay and Kim have a nice analogy for the relationship between the two. R is the
engine of the car, R Studio is the dashboard. The engine does the actual work,
but you would not want to sit on it while driving — you interact with the car
through the dashboard.

Two practical consequences: you need to install R first, and only then can you
install R Studio. And after that you basically only use R Studio; it calls R
whenever necessary, without you having to think about it.

## Slide 16 · R and R packages — the idea

If you install R, you can issue a lot of commands that your computer immediately
understands. However, there might be some routines that R "doesn't understand".

You might "teach" R those by defining, for instance, certain functions that
perform these operations. You might then even "save" these functions and pass
them on to others, so that they can use them as well.

This is exactly the idea of R packages: a collection of variables and functions
written by others that you can install on your computer and then use. Once an R
package is installed, you can use all the functions and variables defined by the
creator of the package.

## Slide 17 · R and R packages — phone & apps

Again, Ismay and Kim have a nice analogy. R is a new phone: useful out of the
box, but most of what you actually do with it comes from the apps you download
from the App Store or Google Play. R packages are those apps.

I wrote a small script that installs all the packages we will use throughout the
semester, so that we can already resolve all installation issues now, in the
first week, rather than in the middle of the term.

## Slide 18 · And what about LaTeX?

In this course we learn how to write nice reports in Quarto: you put R code and
text into one file and get either a webpage in HTML or a nice PDF out of it.

Creating HTML code is easy. Creating a PDF is nothing trivial. To do this we
need a piece of software called LaTeX — a typesetting system that turns plain
text into nicely set text within a PDF document.

You will not have to write LaTeX yourself. But it has to be installed on your
machine, because it is the invisible middle step between your Quarto file and
the finished PDF.

## Slide 19 · Installation procedure

It is absolutely essential that you install all the necessary software as soon
as possible. The installation guidelines are on the course homepage.

Until next session you should have tried to install R, R Studio and Git,
following my tutorials, and you should have posted all problems, with a
screenshot, in the Moodle forum.

Be prepared beforehand: trying to install R just before the session starts is
the fastest way to ruin your day. We need to solve all installation problems by
the end of next week, so post your problems on Moodle and help each other out.

## Slide 20 · Problems with the installation?

If you run into trouble: first check the tutorials again, then post your problem
in Moodle, and always accompany it with a screenshot. Without a screenshot,
nobody can tell what actually went wrong.
